description: Robustness set (Weeks 10-12): 49 harder responses written to stress-test the learner models. Categories: long (multi-sentence answers, some with a buried false belief), mixed (correct idea plus a wrong one, or a self-correction), hedged (uncertainty with no false belief), out_of_catalog (a real misconception that is NOT in the 8-item catalog, so the correct code is null), informal (typos, abbreviations, slang), probe (answers to the 8 probe questions). Labels were written and frozen before any LLM run on this set. baselineCorrect = the grade a lenient binary grader would give by checking for the key fact; rationale explains each label.

responses.label: correct
responses.answer: A server is software (often running on a dedicated computer, but it doesn't have to be) that waits for incoming requests over the network. When a client like a browser or mobile app sends a request, the server processes it, maybe looks something up in a database, and sends a response back. The same machine can even run several servers at once, for example a web server and a database server.
responses.rationale: Complete and accurate; explicitly avoids the hardware-only belief.

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: An API is a set of rules that lets one program talk to another. For example, a weather app on your phone sends a request to a weather service's API and gets back the forecast as JSON. The app doesn't need to know how the service works internally. Basically the API is where all the weather data is kept, so the app is reading straight from it.
responses.rationale: Three correct sentences, then a confident API-is-the-data-store claim at the end. A grader skimming for 'lets programs talk' marks it correct.

responses.label: correct
responses.answer: Authentication answers 'who are you?', for example by checking a password or a fingerprint. Authorization comes after that and answers 'what are you allowed to do?', for example a normal user can view their own orders but only an admin can issue refunds. You can be authenticated and still be denied access to something.

responses.label: partial
responses.answer: Authentication is a security thing that websites do. When you go to a site there's usually a login page, and it's important because hackers try to break into accounts. Lots of sites now also send you a text message with a code. It's all part of keeping the account safe.
responses.rationale: Long and on-topic but never says the key idea (verifying identity). Graded correct because it mentions logging in, like r26.

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: A client is the part of the system that the server pushes information to. The server keeps track of all the connected clients, and whenever it has new pages it sends them out; the client mostly just sits there and displays whatever it gets. Web browsers are an example of a client.
responses.rationale: Correct example (browser) but describes the server as starting the exchange. Graded correct because of the browser example.

responses.label: correct
responses.answer: GET. When you type a URL into the browser it sends a GET request and the server responds with the page. GET requests shouldn't change anything on the server, which is why it's safe to refresh them. POST is what you use when you submit a form to create something.
responses.rationale: Correct, and mentions POST correctly (tests that naming POST is not mistaken for GET/POST confusion).

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: Authorization is about what you are allowed to do once the system knows who you are, like whether you can edit a document or only view it. It's usually set up with roles such as admin or editor. In practice it's handled by your password, since a stronger password gives you more permissions.
responses.rationale: Correct start, then claims the login credential decides permissions.

responses.label: correct
responses.answer: A common way is a username and password: the user types them in, the server checks the password against the stored (hashed) one, and if they match the user is logged in. Many sites also add a second factor, like a code from an authenticator app.

responses.label: correct
responses.answer: In REST, every resource gets its own URL (URI), like /users/42 for one user or /users for the whole collection, and the HTTP method says what to do with that resource.

responses.label: correct
responses.answer: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a contract that says how one piece of software can ask another for data or actions: which requests you can send and what responses you get back. For example, a payments API lets an online shop charge a card without knowing how the bank works internally.

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: A server listens for requests and sends back responses. It has to be a big special computer in a data center though; your laptop can't be a server.
responses.rationale: Correct definition plus a confident hardware-only claim.

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: GET retrieves data. POST also retrieves data, it's just the more secure version of GET.
responses.rationale: Names GET (graded correct) but believes POST is for retrieving data.

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: A password, or using HTTPS, since the encrypted connection also confirms the user's identity.
responses.rationale: Password is correct; HTTPS-proves-identity is the catalog misconception.

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: An API lets programs communicate with each other. It's also the screen with the buttons that the user clicks to use the app.

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: Authentication is checking who you are and authorization is checking what you can do. In practice they're the same step though, because the login system decides both.
responses.rationale: Textbook definitions, then says logging in decides permissions.

responses.label: correct
responses.answer: POST... no wait, POST is for sending data. GET is the one for retrieving it.
responses.rationale: Self-correction: the final answer is right and the student explicitly rejects the wrong idea. Should not be flagged as a misconception.

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: HyperText Transfer Protocol. HTTP is basically the internet itself; without HTTP there would be no internet connection at all.
responses.rationale: Believes HTTP is the internet. Not in the catalog (closest code HTTP_IS_LANGUAGE does not fit).

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: REST identifies resources using the JSON data in the request, since REST APIs always have to use JSON.
responses.rationale: Believes resources are identified by the JSON body and that REST requires JSON. Not in the catalog.

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: Authorization decides what you can access. But it only applies to admins; normal users don't go through authorization at all.
responses.rationale: Believes authorization only applies to admins. Not authn/authz confusion.

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: Authentication is verifying a user's identity. Once you're authenticated on one website, you're automatically authenticated on every other website too.
responses.rationale: Believes authentication is global across sites. Not in the catalog.

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: A server sends responses to clients, but it can only talk to one client at a time, so other users have to wait in line until it's finished.
responses.rationale: Believes a server handles one client at a time. Not the hardware-only or role-reversal belief.

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: GET. But GET requests can't include any parameters, so if you need to search for something you have to use a different method.
responses.rationale: Near-miss: believes GET cannot carry parameters. It does not say POST retrieves data, so GET_POST_CONFUSION would be a forced fit.

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: An API is a programming language, like Python or Java, that's used to build apps.
responses.rationale: Near-miss: believes an API is a programming language. HTTP_IS_LANGUAGE is about HTTP, so it would be a forced fit.

responses.label: misconception
responses.answer: Authentication happens on the client and authorization happens on the server. That's the whole difference.
responses.rationale: Believes the difference is where it runs. Does not claim login decides access, so AUTHN_AUTHZ_CONFUSION would be a forced fit.

responses.answer: False. The client sends the first request, and then the server answers it.

responses.answer: No. HTTP is a protocol, a set of rules for how browsers and servers send requests and responses. Developers write code in languages like JavaScript.

responses.answer: No. The API works behind the scenes so programs can talk to each other; the UI is what people actually see and click.

responses.answer: Yes, if the site has HTTPS then the user must be who they say they are, because the connection is verified.

responses.answer: Not necessarily. Logging in only proves who they are; whether they can delete accounts depends on their permissions, which is authorization.
